episodes.190583: Mid-level monsoon moisture was rotating around an upper level high pressure system centered in Central Texas. This moisture combined with low level convergence in a surface pressure trough to create isolated thunderstorms across the extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle on the afternoon of the eighth. One of these storms produced quarter size hail near the town of Rhea in far northwestern Parmer County.
episodes.190671: A high influx of moisture ahead of an approaching upper low over the bootheel of NM allowed numerous showers and thunderstorms to develop over central and eastern NM on June 9th. Slow storm motions resulted from a decaying high pressure system still centered over northern NM, allowing storms to produce locally heavy rainfall. A series of three such slow moving storms passed over southeastern Albuquerque during the late afternoon hours, dumping 2 to 3 inches of rain in a small area near and just west of the Four Hills development. Flash flooding resulted, and swift water rescues were performed in two locations. There was unfortunately one death in a diversion channel from the fast moving waters, while two others were rescued.||Key Words: Hail, Flash Flood.
episodes.190834: On the afternoon of the ninth, thunderstorms initially developed along a low-level boundary cutting west to east across the central South Plains and Rolling Plains, fueled by deep, rich moisture and a weakness aloft. Numerous outflow boundaries developed across the South Plains region further sparking additional showers and thunderstorm growth. Although vertical wind shear was weak, decent instability did allow several storms to become strong to briefly severe. Pea to quarter size hail fell in a number of locations, including the south side of Lubbock (Lubbock County) and over Ralls (Crosby County), while several wind gusts in excess of 50 mph were observed. One severe gust of 67 mph was measured at the Lubbock International Airport. More significantly, the abundant moisture supported efficient rain rates and widespread robust rain totals which did lead to pockets of flash flooding. Several reports of street flooding and vehicles stranded were received from in and around Lubbock as a couple different rounds of very heavy rain targeted the area.
episodes.190849: A gust front produced localized gale-force wind gusts over the tidal Potomac River.
episodes.190950: A supercell developed in the late evening of June 8th as upper level ascent passed over southern Missouri. This supercell caused wind damage in Reynolds County before exiting the forecast area to the southeast.
episodes.191067: Slow moving thunderstorms produced hail and heavy rainfall as they slowly drift south across the east/southeast part of the Denver Metro area. Additional storms track across Colorado producing hail up to 1 inch in Fairplay and Platteville. Plowable hail occurred under the Fairplay storm.
episodes.191105: A line of thunderstorms tracked southeast across the eastern Colorado plains during the afternoon and early evening of June 8th. The line of storms produce some severe hail, but strong winds were the main impact from the storms. Storm chasers encountered very strong winds at times with estimated wind gusts up to 100 mph. There were reports of branches broken off trees and some power line poles snapped.
episodes.191223: Two rounds of thunderstorms affected the Missouri Ozarks beginning on the evening of June 8th and continued through the morning of June 9th. Severe thunderstorms with large hail and damaging winds occurred with both rounds. Significant flash flooding occurred overnight where 3-6 inches of rainfall occurred. Numerous water rescues occurred.
episodes.191538: With a surface trough across the Florida Peninsula, there were conditions ideal for morning development of waterspouts on June 9th. There were occasional weak showers and fair weather cumulus over the Atlantic providing the environment prime off the eastern coast.
episodes.191722: In the afternoon of the 8th, multiple storms began forming across eastern Colorado. These storms varied in their speed and strength, but overall eastern Colorado experienced baseball sized hail, flash flooding, a tornado, and straight line wind damage with observed speeds of 97 MPH and estimated speeds over 110 MPH.  No damage was observed from the tornado.
episodes.191941: Scattered strong to severe storms developed producing large hail and wind damage. The majority of reports were over central Arkansas during the afternoon to late afternoon hours.
episodes.192065: A cold front moving through the region sparked a broken line of thunderstorms, of which a couple of storms produced isolated pockets of severe straight line wind damage.
episodes.192599: An organized linear complex of thunderstorms, centered across south-central Kansas, produced a severe-caliber wind gust across far northern Oklahoma during the early morning of the 9th. Additional diurnally-driven convection across southern Oklahoma produced localized flooding and a report of large hail during the evening.
episodes.192644: In the afternoon of the 8th, storms developed in eastern Colorado and proceeded into western Kansas in the later afternoon and early evening. Winds up to 70 MPH and 1.25 inch hail were reported.
episodes.192870: Afternoon instability combined with a passing trough caused a line of thunderstorms to develop that became strong over Lake Erie. They weakened as they tracked inland.
episodes.192944: During the evening and into the overnight of the 8th, a complex of strong to severe thunderstorms came through central and southern Kansas.  High winds up to 75 to 80 mph occurred with numerous reports of downed tree limbs and power lines.  Very heavy rain occurred with this complex of storms causing flooding in southeast Kansas.
episodes.193089: High winds and heavy rain reported 06/09.
episodes.193093: Scattered thunderstorms developed across west central Arkansas during the afternoon of the 9th, as a cold front moved through the region. The strongest storms produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.193189: A cold front moved south from northern Missouri during the evening hours of June 8, 2024. A mesoscale convective system developed along and in advance of the front in the moist and unstable airmass across southern Missouri. There was enough shear across the area to support a few severe storms. This convection pushed across northern parts of the Mid-South mainly during the early morning hours of June 9, 2024, with isolated reports of hail and damaging winds.

There was enough shear across the area to support a few severe storms. This convection pushed across northern parts of the Mid-South mainly during the early morning hours of June 9, 2024, with isolated reports of hail and damaging winds.

There was enough shear across the area to support a few severe storms. episodes.193194: Storms developed across northeast Mississippi along an outflow boundary generated from earlier convection.  This outflow boundary interacted with an extremely unstable atmosphere. Surface-based convective available potential energy values exceed 4000 J/kg. Storm organization was helped by 0-6km wind shear values that exceeded 30 knots. Several supercells developed with numerous reports of large hail. Some storms split into right and left movers, each producing large hail.
episodes.193374: A line of training storms over east central Kansas during the early morning hours on the 9th resulted in 2 to 4 inches of rainfall.  Several road closures were reported in Lyon and Anderson counties.
episodes.193464: A boundary stalled out over the plains and resulted in the development of strong storms. Heavy rainfall from thunderstorms produced some flash flooding in Huerfano and Pueblo Counties. Isolated stronger storms (sub-severe) also developed further west over Saguache County, resulting in some hail (below severe criteria) and a brief landspout was also reported.
episodes.193540: Several reports of severe weather were received through the afternoon.
episodes.193635: A large negatively tilted trough to the west of the southern Great Plains and a stalled cold front resulted in numerous afternoon thunderstorms across the region. A few of these thunderstorms produced severe wind gusts.
episodes.193732: A weakening line of thunderstorms moved into western North Carolina from east Tennessee during the evening. Brief, isolated strong to damaging wind gusts were reported.
episodes.193912: A shortwave moving over the region produced two days of severe storms, which resulted in winds of severe criteria at both the Pueblo and Lamar airports, and also some wind damage in Canon City.
episodes.194273: Rivers on the North Slope began to open up during late May. An ice jam on the Kuparuk River formed downstream of Spine Road. A surge of high water caused by warm temperatures and snow melt in the Brooks Range was backed up behind the ice jam, causing flooding in low-lying and flood prone locations, as well as the low-water crossings approaching the bridges over the Kuparuk River.

On June 7th at 1500 AKDT, a USGS hydro technician observed an ice jam downstream of Spine road. The Kupurak Roads and Pads Foreman reported that the causeway approaches to bridges were flooded and that water went over the road on Sunday June 9th and rose Sunday night with an estimated 0.5 feet of water on the road. Water levels at the KUPA2 (Kuparuk River near Deadhorse) gage hit minor flood stage of 35.5 feet on Sunday June 9th at 0500 AKDT and rose steadily until early afternoon. There was a steep rise from mid-afternoon through 1900 AKDT to a relatively flat plateau around 36.7 feet.  The Kuparuk Roads and Pads Foreman reported water was 0.7 feet deep over the road and that vehicles were being escorted across. On June 11th at 1200 AKDT the sate at KUPA2 was around 36.3 feet. Water levels remained above minor flood stage until late morning on June 12 when recession steepened, and fell below action state by the morning of June 13th.

Numerous thunderstorms grew upscale on the evening of the ninth due to several outflow boundaries. A very moist atmosphere allowed storms to produce heavy rainfall in addition to severe hail and winds. One of these storms moved over Lubbock County producing rain rates between three to five inches per hour. This caused many roads in and around the city of Lubbock to become impassable to due water over the roadway. There was a brief lull in activity between storms around 1800 CST through 2030 CST. An additional thunderstorm after 2030 CST again produced flash flooding due to heavy rainfall.
